//: Which drawing in which source file is which species. `group` is the index of a top-level <g> in the file - run `npm run animal-art -- --index` to print a labelled contact sheet and read the numbers off it. `flip` mirrors a drawing so every animal in the game faces the same way (right).

sources.//: No usable groups on this sheet, so the birds are found as islands. `drop` removes the sheet's own teal shadow puddle, which would otherwise sit on the grass. `unitScale` puts this sheet's units on the same scale as the first one: not by biology - the sheet draws small animals two to four times life size, so a flamingo sized truthfully looks shrunken beside an inflated fox. It is set to sit where the sheet would have drawn it.

A jungle scene: every animal sits among the same foliage, so islands weld them together and each is named by the patch it occupies instead. The parrot stands alone and comes out as an island. No gorilla here - the apes on this sheet are chimpanzees, and labelling one a gorilla would be a lie the game repeats to a room full of people.

Each animal sits on a pale blob the colour of the sheet's own backdrop, so that colour is dropped. The gorilla is taken by region rather than as an island: its body alone is a fifth of the page, and the island finder treats anything that big as scenery.
Drawn three-quarter on rather than in profile like the other sheets, so only taken where the pose earns it. A sitting panda reads as a sitting panda from any angle.

Flat, side on, no outlines - the closest match yet to the first sheet. Only the two species the game was missing are taken; the rest duplicate what is already drawn. The meerkat carries its own scale: this sheet draws one nearly as tall as a lion, which is a poster's convention rather than a park's.
The same hand as savanna.svg. Each species carries its own scale: the sheet draws an impala nearly as tall as a buffalo, which a poster does and a park cannot.
A sheet of otters. The walking profile is the one a park wants - the others are floating, curled or head-on, which read as a portrait rather than an animal in an enclosure.

Reef fish. This sheet keeps its colours in a <style> block and gives every shape a class, so it only works because the extractor now writes the computed styling onto the elements first. Without that it comes out a correctly shaped, entirely black fish.

A page of birds. The peacock is taken displaying and front on, which breaks the side-view rule the way the sitting panda does: a peacock in display is drawn from the front by everyone, because that is the whole point of it. The eagle is in profile like the rest.

A lion family, and the whole pride comes from THIS one sheet on purpose: a male, a lioness and a cub drawn by three different hands standing in one habitat would look like three different animals. The male is an island of his own; the lioness and the cub are cut from the cluster in the middle by the patch each occupies. Standing poses for all three, so they read as one family rather than one walking and one sitting for no reason.

Emu and kangaroo, the last two species the toolbox offered and nobody had drawn. ignoreLargerThan is 0.15 here, not the usual 0.06: the kangaroo is the biggest animal on a small sheet and its body was being taken for background, which left an island of pale legs and no kangaroo at all. These two are drawn WITH an outline and the rest of the menagerie is not - the outline is filled shapes rather than strokes, so it cannot be taken off without taking the eyes and the nostrils with it. They read as the same animals in the same zoo, a little more boldly drawn.
